questions.prompt: What is the default lifecycle behavior of closure parameters in Swift?

options.text: They are non-escaping and execute before the function returns.
options.explanation: Right. Closure parameters in Swift are non-escaping by default, executing synchronously within the function body.

options.text: They are escaping and allocated permanently on the heap.
options.explanation: Escaping closures require an explicit @escaping annotation.

options.text: They capture all surrounding variables as weak references.
options.explanation: Closures capture variables strongly by reference unless a capture list is specified.

options.text: They run automatically on background concurrency queues.
options.explanation: Closures execute on the calling thread unless scheduled on a queue explicitly.

questions.prompt: When is a closure considered an escaping closure in Swift?

options.text: When it accepts more than two parameters from callers.
options.explanation: The number of parameters does not dictate closure escaping behavior.

options.text: When it is called after the enclosing function returns.
options.explanation: Right. An escaping closure is passed into a function but executes after the function body has returned.

options.text: When it is declared as a private method inside a struct.
options.explanation: Private methods are member declarations, not escaping closure arguments.

options.text: When it mutates value types using the inout keyword.
options.explanation: inout parameters are evaluated during function execution, not after return.

questions.prompt: Where does Swift allocate non-escaping closures in memory?

options.text: In static global application data storage.
options.explanation: Static data storage is used for global variables, not short-lived closures.

options.text: On the garbage collected runtime pool.
options.explanation: Swift uses Automatic Reference Counting, not a garbage collector.

options.text: On the local function call stack.
options.explanation: Right. Non-escaping closures cannot outlive the enclosing function call, so they are allocated on the stack.

options.text: In a dedicated external framework bundle.
options.explanation: Bundles contain resources and compiled binaries, not runtime closure instances.

questions.prompt: Which keyword attribute must be added to a closure parameter that is stored for later execution?

options.text: The @autoclosure attribute.
options.explanation: @autoclosure automatically wraps an expression in a closure without escaping it.

options.text: The @discardableResult attribute.
options.explanation: @discardableResult suppresses compiler warnings when a function return value is unused.

options.text: The @convention attribute.
options.explanation: @convention specifies the calling convention (such as c or block).

options.text: The @escaping attribute.
options.explanation: Right. @escaping tells the compiler that the closure may outlive the function call.

questions.prompt: How does a closure capture variables from surrounding scope by default?

options.text: By reference, reading the current value when executing.
options.explanation: Right. By default, closures capture variables by reference, observing any mutations made before execution.

options.text: By creating an immutable value copy at declaration.
options.explanation: Creating an immutable copy requires an explicit capture list like [count].

options.text: By boxing every variable into an optional weak pointer.
options.explanation: Weak references require explicit capture lists and only apply to class types.

options.text: By converting all referenced types into reference types.
options.explanation: Swift does not change the underlying type of value types.

questions.prompt: What happens when an escaping closure captures self strongly and is stored on self?

options.text: The compiler releases the closure upon dismissal.
options.explanation: ARC cannot automatically break strong reference cycles between objects.

options.text: A strong retain cycle occurs, preventing deallocation.
options.explanation: Right. The instance retains the closure and the closure retains the instance, creating a memory leak.

options.text: The class instance is converted into a value type.
options.explanation: Classes remain reference types on the heap regardless of capture.

options.text: The closure executes immediately on the main thread.
options.explanation: Retain cycles affect memory retention, not execution timing or thread scheduling.

questions.prompt: What does the capture list [weak self] do inside a closure?

options.text: It turns self into an unowned non-optional reference.
options.explanation: unowned creates a non-optional reference, whereas weak creates an optional reference.

options.text: It forces the closure to run synchronously on stack.
options.explanation: Capture lists govern memory reference semantics, not execution synchronicity.

options.text: It captures self as an optional that becomes nil at exit.
options.explanation: Right. [weak self] captures self weakly as an optional, and ARC zeroes it to nil if the instance deallocates.

options.text: It prevents other threads from accessing self directly.
options.explanation: weak references do not provide thread synchronization or locks.

questions.prompt: Why is [unowned self] risky for asynchronous network completion handlers?

options.text: unowned references cannot access any stored properties.
options.explanation: unowned references access properties identically to strong references.

options.text: The compiler rejects unowned references in callbacks.
options.explanation: The compiler permits unowned references, but they are unsafe if the object deallocates.

options.text: unowned references consume twice as much memory space.
options.explanation: unowned references have negligible overhead and do not consume double memory.

options.text: It crashes at runtime if the instance has deallocated.
options.explanation: Right. unowned assumes the instance is always alive; accessing it after deallocation causes a fatal crash.

questions.prompt: What is the standard pattern to safely use a weak self reference inside a closure body?

options.text: guard let self = self else { return }
options.explanation: Right. This safely unwraps the optional weak reference and ensures self stays alive for the closure scope.

options.text: try self!.performOperationAction()
options.explanation: Force unwrapping self! causes crashes if the instance has deallocated.

options.text: fatalError(self.descriptionText)
options.explanation: fatalError terminates the application intentionally.

options.text: assert(self != nil, "Failed ref")
options.explanation: Assertions are disabled in production release builds and do not unwrap optionals.

questions.prompt: What does writing [count] in a closure capture list do when count is an Int variable?

options.text: It allows the closure to mutate count in the scope.
options.explanation: The captured variable inside the closure is an immutable constant.

options.text: It captures an immutable snapshot of count at start.
options.explanation: Right. Capture lists take an immutable snapshot copy of value types at the moment the closure is created.

options.text: It converts count into a mutable reference pointer.
options.explanation: Default capture captures by reference; capture lists capture an immutable copy.

options.text: It makes count optional inside the closure body.
options.explanation: Value types in capture lists remain non-optional.

questions.prompt: Why do non-escaping closures not cause retain cycles with self?

options.text: Non-escaping closures cannot reference classes.
options.explanation: Non-escaping closures can freely reference class instances and properties.

options.text: The compiler forces all references to be weak.
options.explanation: References inside non-escaping closures remain strong.

options.text: They execute and finish before the function exits.
options.explanation: Right. Non-escaping closures are released as soon as the function returns, so no cycle can persist.

options.text: They run exclusively inside background task groups.
options.explanation: Non-escaping closures run synchronously on the calling thread.

questions.prompt: What compiler error occurs if you assign a non-escaping closure parameter to a stored property?

options.text: error: closure must return an optional value.
options.explanation: Return types do not influence escaping validation.

options.text: error: cannot convert value to closure type.
options.explanation: The types match, but the lifetime semantics conflict.

options.text: error: closures must be marked with mutating.
options.explanation: mutating applies to methods on structs, not escaping attributes.

options.text: error: assigning non-escaping to '@escaping'.
options.explanation: Right. Swift forbids storing non-escaping closures in properties that outlive the call.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift require explicit self inside escaping closures?

options.text: To make developers acknowledge reference capture.
options.explanation: Right. Swift forces explicit self so developers are reminded that the closure will capture and retain self.

options.text: Because the compiler cannot resolve method names.
options.explanation: The compiler can resolve names; the rule exists purely for capture clarity.

options.text: To force the compiler to allocate code on stack.
options.explanation: Escaping closures are allocated on the heap regardless of self syntax.

options.text: To enable Objective-C dynamic method resolution.
options.explanation: Swift uses static and vtable dispatch, not dynamic Objective-C resolution by default.

questions.prompt: Which of the following closures is non-escaping by default in the Swift Standard Library?

options.text: The DispatchQueue async function.
options.explanation: DispatchQueue.async takes an @escaping closure because it runs on a queue later.

options.text: The Array map transformation method.
options.explanation: Right. Array.map executes its closure synchronously on elements before returning.

options.text: The UIView animate block function.
options.explanation: UIView animation blocks escape to be executed by the Core Animation engine.

options.text: The Timer scheduled timer method.
options.explanation: Timers execute closures repeatedly or after a time delay, escaping the initial setup call.

questions.prompt: How did Swift 5.3 improve the ergonomics of self inside closures with capture lists?

options.text: It removed the need for weak references in calls.
options.explanation: Weak references are still necessary to prevent retain cycles.

options.text: It converted unowned references to weak pointers.
options.explanation: unowned references remain distinct from weak references.

options.text: It allowed implicit self when self is in capture.
options.explanation: Right. SE-0269 allowed omitting self. inside closure bodies when self is listed in the capture list.

options.text: It banned strong self captures across all scopes.
options.explanation: Strong captures are still permitted when explicitly requested.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between escaping and non-escaping closures in Swift. When must a closure parameter be marked @escaping? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that non-escaping closures execute synchronously within the function body before returning
Explains that escaping closures outlive the function call, such as when stored in properties or passed to async callbacks

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, closure parameters are non-escaping by default, meaning they execute synchronously within the function body before the function returns. A closure must be marked @escaping when it outlives the function that received it. Common examples include stored properties and asynchronous callbacks. Escaping closures are allocated on the heap rather than the stack.

questions.prompt: What is a strong reference cycle between a class instance and a closure, and how does [weak self] prevent it? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains how a retain cycle forms when an instance retains a closure that captures the instance strongly
Explains that [weak self] creates an optional weak reference that avoids incrementing retain count and zeroes on deallocation

questions.modelAnswer: A strong reference cycle occurs when a class instance holds a strong reference to an escaping closure, and that closure captures the instance strongly. Because each holds a retain count on the other, neither can ever be deallocated by ARC. Using [weak self] breaks this cycle by capturing an optional weak reference that does not increment retain count and becomes nil when the instance deallocates.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: Compare [weak self] and [unowned self] in Swift closure capture lists. Why is [weak self] generally preferred for asynchronous callbacks? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that weak creates an optional reference zeroed on deallocation, while unowned assumes the instance is always alive
Explains that unowned crashes if the instance deallocates before asynchronous callback execution

questions.modelAnswer: Both weak and unowned break retain cycles by not increasing the retain count of the captured instance. However, weak captures self as an optional that ARC zeroes to nil upon deallocation, while unowned assumes the instance will never be deallocated. Weak self is preferred for asynchronous callbacks. If a user dismisses a screen before a network call completes, unowned self causes a fatal crash.

questions.prompt: How does capturing a value type in a closure capture list differ from capturing it without a capture list? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that default capture is by reference and reflects subsequent changes to the variable
Explains that capture lists take an immutable snapshot copy of value types at closure creation time

questions.modelAnswer: By default, a closure captures variables from surrounding scope by reference, meaning it observes changes made to the variable after the closure is declared. When a value type is included in a capture list like [count], Swift captures an immutable copy of its current value at declaration time. Subsequent changes to the outer variable do not affect the captured copy inside the closure.

questions.prompt: Why does the Swift compiler require explicit self inside escaping closures, and how does this requirement protect developers? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that explicit self requires developers to acknowledge capturing the enclosing instance
Explains that it prevents accidental retain cycles and memory leaks in escaping closures

questions.modelAnswer: The Swift compiler requires explicit self inside escaping closures to make sure developers consciously acknowledge that the closure captures reference semantics. Because escaping closures outlive their calling scope and can create retain cycles, requiring self. or [weak self] makes memory capture explicit. This warning prevents accidental memory leaks caused by unintentionally retaining the enclosing class instance.
